newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - History warns British Liberals of coalition peril.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - History warns British Liberals of coalition peril.

text.p: Britain's Liberal Democrats, heirs to a proud political tradition, are pondering an uncomfortable historical dilemma.
Do they support a likely Labour government after the next general election or should they heed the lessons of the past and stay aloof?
Britain's third political force was pithily reminded of the dangers of alliances during its party conference last month.
"In British politics, minnows swimming in the same tank with pike have always been gobbled up," said one delegate.
But although the old Liberals have amply demonstrated this century how true that remark is, some party members feel that this time they might reap real gains through a pact.

Party leader Paddy Ashdown says he rules nothing out on the question of whether he will swim in the same governmental water as Tony Blair if the Labour leader falls short of an overall majority at the election due by May.

But some colleagues are more enthusiastic. One Liberal MP, Alex Carlile, called on Ashdown to respond positively to any approach from Blair who has pulled his party towards the centre ground of politics -- traditional Liberal country -- since becoming leader in July 1994.
Elder statesman Lord Bill Rodgers even urged Liberals in some constituencies to consider voting Labour if the Labour candidate had a better chance of beating the Conservative.
These calls are inspired by the desperate need, as the centre and left of British politics sees it, for a clean break with 17 years of Conservative rule.

Indeed, some Liberals now argue that in many of their policies, they are to the left of Labour, citing a willingness to raise taxes on high earners, and to increase spending on health and education which contrasts with Labour "timidity".

"There is one thing that our two parties have in common," Liberal president Bob Maclennan told delegates at the conference. "We are not the Conservatives. Between us and Labour this is not the time for poison blowpipes or battle axes."
Yet from the viewpoint of party advantage, the historical precedents are every bit as dire as the Liberal councillor's warnings about the future.
It was a coalition which destroyed the old Liberal Party as one of the two governing parties of Britain.

The Liberals and Conservatives worked together in government during World War One under Liberal David Lloyd George, a fiery silver-tongued Welshman who just years previously had been reviled by every "Tory" in the land as a dangerous radical.
After the war was over, Lloyd George called a general election in which some Liberals campaigned for a continuation of the coalition into peacetime and others opposed it.
The party split proved irrevocable, membership plummetted, organisation fell apart and policy atrophied into little but a determined defence of the principle of free trade.

By 1924, the Liberal Party, which at the 1906 general election had won the largest majority ever recorded in British politics for a single party, was a bedraggled rump with just 40 seats in a House of Commons of more than 600 members.

A World War Two coalition gave Sir Archibald Sinclair a place in Winston Churchill's government as Air Force minister, making him the last British Liberal to have sat round the Downing Street cabinet table.
But for the party, it spelt only doom. Liberals tumbled to 12, then nine, then six seats in the House of Commons.

Since then, the Liberals, ever flying around the fringes of political power and gradually increasing their parliamentary strength to its present 25 MPs, have allowed their wings to be singed just once by cooperation with a larger party.
The "Lib-Lab pact" of 1977-8 saw the party propping up a Labour government which had lost its parliamentary majority in exchange for consultation on parliamentary bills.
The Liberals immediately began to perform abysmally in local council elections and parliamentary by-elections.
In his book on the pact, then Liberal leader David Steel said he believed it had been worth it to provide Britain with stable government and achieve some limited Liberal objectives.
He added: "The most obvious defect...was the one forecast by the doubters in our own ranks, namely that the failure and unpopularity of the Labour government rubbed off on us."
The pact ended a few months before the 1979 election, and the Liberals' poll ratings gradually improved.
Clearly Blair sees the Liberals as a possible prop on the path to power -- if he needs them. But why do some Liberals imagine a coalition could be different next time?
"I personally am happy to contemplate such an arrangement," said MP Menzies Campbell. "But its purpose would be to ensure the prevailing of Liberal Democrat policies."
Liberals sympathetic to coalition -- perhaps half the party -- claim this is what it has achieved in several deals with Labour on "hung" local councils throughout Britain.
They name the policies they would stress at the national level as things such as boosting spending on education, or shaking up Britain's constitution.

But for self-interest, there is one long-treasured policy which would have to feature in any Liberal list setting out the price of their support -- proportional representation -- something on which Blair is willing to contemplate a referendum.
At the last general election, the Liberals won 17.8 percent of the votes but just over three percent of the seats fought.

If a big partner could assure them that in exchange for their entering a coalition, it would scrap Britain's first-past-the-post voting system, then the party's worries about the deal losing it support would be greatly soothed.
"We would have found the key to eternal life as a party," said one parliamentary candidate. "You don't have to be Faust to be willing to sell a small part of your soul for that."
